q: A gaming company is building an application with Voice over IP capabilities. The application will serve traffic to users across the world. The application needs to be highly available with an automated failover across AWS Regions. The company wants to minimize the latency of users without relying on IP address caching on user devices. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

o.t: Use AWS Global Accelerator with health checks.
o.w: Global Accelerator uses static Anycast IP addresses and continuously monitors endpoint health, automatically routing traffic over the AWS global network to the closest healthy Region, eliminating the need for clients to cache or re-resolve IP addresses on failover.

o.t: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that includes multiple origins.
o.w: CloudFront is built for cacheable HTTP(S) content delivery, not low-latency VoIP traffic, and it does not provide the fast, DNS-independent Regional failover that this real-time application needs.

o.t: Create an Application Load Balancer that uses path-based routing.
o.w: An ALB operates within a single Region and cannot route traffic across AWS Regions, so it cannot provide automated cross-Region failover for a globally distributed VoIP application.

o.t: Use Amazon Route 53 with a geolocation routing policy.
o.w: Route 53 geolocation routing relies on DNS resolution and TTL-based caching on client devices, so failover is delayed until the cached DNS record expires, violating the requirement to avoid relying on IP caching.

explain: AWS Global Accelerator is a service that provides static IP addresses (Anycast) to route traffic over the AWS global network. It routes traffic over the optimal path to the AWS endpoint, improving availability and performance.

q: A company’s facility has badge readers at every entrance throughout the building. When badges are scanned, the readers send a message over HTTPS to indicate who attempted to access that particular entrance. A solutions architect must design a system to process these messages from the sensors. The solution must be highly available, and the results must be made available for the company’s security team to analyze. Which system architecture should the solutions architect recommend?

o.t: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3. Configure a Site-to-Site VPN connection from the facility network to the VPC so that sensor data can be written directly to an S3 bucket by way of the VPC endpoint.
o.w: A gateway VPC endpoint only provides private routing to S3 from inside a VPC; it cannot serve as a public HTTPS endpoint for badge readers, and writing raw messages straight to S3 provides no processing or easy querying for the security team.

o.t: Launch an Amazon EC2 instance to serve as the HTTPS endpoint and to process the messages. Configure the EC2 instance to save the results to an Amazon S3 bucket.
o.w: A single EC2 instance is a single point of failure unless placed behind a load balancer and Auto Scaling group, and self-managing the HTTPS endpoint adds operational overhead that a managed solution avoids.

o.t: Create an HTTPS endpoint in Amazon API Gateway. Configure the API Gateway endpoint to invoke an AWS Lambda function to process the messages and save the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table.
o.w: API Gateway provides a highly available, scalable HTTPS endpoint, and integrating it with Lambda to process messages and store structured results in DynamoDB gives the security team an easily queryable, durable store, fully managed with built-in redundancy.

o.t: Use Amazon Route 53 to direct incoming sensor messages to an AWS Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to process the messages and save the results to an Amazon DynamoDB table.
o.w: Amazon Route 53 is a DNS service; it cannot directly receive and route HTTPS messages to a Lambda function the way an API Gateway endpoint can.

q: A company has a custom application with embedded credentials that retrieves information from an Amazon RDS MySQL DB instance. Management says the application must be made more secure with the least amount of programming effort. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

o.t: Create credentials on the RDS for MySQL database for the application user and store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Secrets Manager. Set up a credentials rotation schedule for the application user in the RDS for MySQL database using Secrets Manager.
o.w: Secrets Manager natively stores the database credentials and includes built-in, managed rotation for RDS MySQL via AWS-provided Lambda rotation templates, so the application loads credentials dynamically with essentially no custom rotation code.

o.t: Create credentials on the RDS for MySQL database for the application user and store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Secrets Manager. Create an AWS Lambda function that rotates the credentials in Secret Manager.
o.w: Secrets Manager already provides built-in rotation templates for RDS MySQL, so writing a custom Lambda function to rotate credentials duplicates functionality and adds unnecessary programming effort.

o.t: Create credentials on the RDS for MySQL database for the application user and store the credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Configure the application to load the database credentials from Parameter Store. Set up a credentials rotation schedule for the application user in the RDS for MySQL database using Parameter Store.
o.w: Parameter Store does not have native, built-in automatic credential rotation for RDS the way Secrets Manager does; achieving rotation would require custom scripting, increasing programming effort.

o.t: Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) to create keys. Configure the application to load the database credentials from AWS KMS. Enable automatic key rotation.
o.w: AWS KMS manages encryption keys, not database credentials; it has no concept of a MySQL username/password and cannot be used by the application to retrieve or rotate database login credentials.

explain: C is a valid solution for securing the custom application with the least amount of programming effort. It involves creating credentials on the RDS for MySQL database for the application user and storing them in AWS Secrets Manager. The application can then be configured to load the database credentials from Secrets Manager. Additionally, the solution includes setting up a credentials rotation schedule for the application user in the RDS for MySQL database using Secrets Manager, which will automatically rotate the credentials at a specified interval without requiring any programming effort.

q: A company has a stateless web application that runs on AWS Lambda functions that are invoked by Amazon API Gateway. The company wants to deploy the application across multiple AWS Regions to provide Regional failover capabilities. What should a solutions architect do to route traffic to multiple Regions?

o.t: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an origin for each Region. Use CloudFront health checks to route traffic.
o.w: CloudFront health checks exist, but CloudFront is a content delivery/caching layer, not a DNS failover mechanism designed for routing API traffic between independent Regional API Gateway deployments.

o.t: Create an Application Load Balancer in the primary Region. Set the target group to point to the API Gateway endpoint hostnames in each Region.
o.w: An Application Load Balancer cannot target an API Gateway endpoint hostname as a registered target, and keeping the ALB only in the primary Region reintroduces a single point of failure.

o.t: Create Amazon Route 53 health checks for each Region. Use an active-active failover configuration.
o.w: Route 53 health checks combined with an active-active failover routing policy continuously monitor each Regional API Gateway endpoint and automatically route traffic only to healthy Regions, giving true Regional failover for a stateless API.

o.t: Create a transit gateway. Attach the transit gateway to the API Gateway endpoint in each Region. Configure the transit gateway to route requests.
o.w: A transit gateway operates at the network (VPC) layer to connect VPCs and on-premises networks; it has no way to attach to or route traffic to a serverless API Gateway endpoint.

explain: By creating Amazon Route 53 health checks for each Region and configuring an active-active failover configuration, Route 53 can monitor the health of the endpoints in each Region and route traffic to healthy endpoints. In the event of a failure in one Region, Route 53 automatically routes traffic to the healthy endpoints in other Regions.

q: A solutions architect needs to design a system to store client case files. The files are core company assets and are important. The number of files will grow over time. The files must be simultaneously accessible from multiple application servers that run on Amazon EC2 instances. The solution must have built-in redundancy. Which solution meets these requirements?

o.t: Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
o.w: Amazon EBS volumes attach to a single EC2 instance at a time (with limited exceptions) and cannot be mounted concurrently by multiple application servers as a general shared file system.

o.t: AWS Backup
o.w: AWS Backup is a backup and recovery service, not a storage service; it cannot serve as the primary, concurrently-accessible storage layer for active case files.

o.t: Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS)
o.w: Amazon EFS is a fully managed, elastic NFS file system that can be mounted simultaneously by many EC2 instances across Availability Zones, and it stores data redundantly across multiple AZs by design.

o.t: Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive
o.w: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is designed for rarely-accessed archival data with retrieval times of hours, not for files that must be simultaneously and readily accessible from multiple application servers.

q: A solutions architect is designing a highly available Amazon ElastiCache for Redis based solution. The solutions architect needs to ensure that failures do not result in performance degradation or loss of data locally and within an AWS Region. The solution needs to provide high availability at the node level and at the Region level. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Use Multi-AZ Redis replication groups with shards that contain multiple nodes.
o.w: Multi-AZ replication groups keep a failover-capable read replica in a different AZ for each shard, so a node or AZ failure triggers automatic failover with minimal data loss, while sharding distributes load to avoid performance degradation.

o.t: Use Redis shards that contain multiple nodes with Redis append only files (AOF) turned on.
o.w: Append-only file (AOF) persistence helps with data durability on a single node restart but does not provide the automatic Multi-AZ failover needed to protect against node or AZ-level failures without performance impact.

o.t: Use a Multi-AZ Redis cluster with more than one read replica in the replication group.
o.w: Simply adding more read replicas within a cluster without Multi-AZ placement does not protect against an Availability Zone outage, since all nodes could still reside in, or depend on, the same AZ failing together.

o.t: Use Redis shards that contain multiple nodes with Auto Scaling turned on.
o.w: Auto Scaling for ElastiCache adjusts capacity to handle load but does not by itself provide the automatic cross-AZ failover needed to avoid data loss and performance degradation during a node failure.

explain:
Multi-AZ (Availability Zone) replication groups provide high availability at the node level. In a Multi-AZ setup, your data is replicated asynchronously to a standby replica in a different Availability Zone.
Using shards with multiple nodes within each Availability Zone further enhances availability and provides scalability.

q: A company wants to run an in-memory database for a latency-sensitive application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. The application processes more than 100,000 transactions each minute and requires high network throughput. A solutions architect needs to provide a costeffective network design that minimizes data transfer charges. Which solution meets these requirements?

o.t: Deploy an Auto Scaling group with a step scaling policy to launch EC2 instances in different Availability Zones.
o.w: Spreading instances across multiple Availability Zones via Auto Scaling increases inter-AZ data transfer charges and added latency, which directly conflicts with the goal of minimizing network costs for a latency-sensitive workload.

o.t: Launch all EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone within the same AWS Region. Specify a placement group with cluster strategy when launching EC2 instances.
o.w: A cluster placement group packs instances close together within a single AZ on the same low-latency, high-throughput network fabric, and keeping everything in one AZ avoids the data transfer charges that apply to cross-AZ traffic.

o.t: Launch all EC2 instances in different Availability Zones within the same AWS Region. Specify a placement group with partition strategy when launching EC2 instances.
o.w: A partition placement group spreads instances across separate racks/AZs to limit the impact of hardware failures, which increases cross-AZ latency and data transfer costs rather than minimizing them.

o.t: Deploy an Auto Scaling group to launch EC2 instances in different Availability Zones based on a network utilization target.
o.w: Scaling instances across different AZs based on network utilization still incurs cross-AZ data transfer charges and added latency, failing to meet the cost-minimization and high-throughput requirements.

explain:
A placement group is a logical grouping of instances within a single Availability Zone. The "cluster" strategy for placement groups places instances in close proximity to each other, providing low-latency, high-throughput communication between instances.
By launching all EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone within the same AWS Region, you minimize data transfer charges because data transfer within the same Availability Zone is not subject to additional costs.

q: A company is making a prototype of the infrastructure for its new website by manually provisioning the necessary infrastructure. This infrastructure includes an Auto Scaling group, an Application Load Balancer and an Amazon RDS database. After the configuration has been thoroughly validated, the company wants the capability to immediately deploy the infrastructure for development and production use in two Availability Zones in an automated fashion. What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?

o.t: Define the infrastructure as a template by using the prototype infrastructure as a guide. Deploy the infrastructure with AWS CloudFormation.
o.w: AWS CloudFormation lets you codify the validated infrastructure (Auto Scaling group, ALB, RDS) as a reusable template and deploy identical stacks repeatedly and automatically across environments and Availability Zones.

o.t: Use AWS Config to record the inventory of resources that are used in the prototype infrastructure. Use AWS Config to deploy the prototype infrastructure into two Availability Zones.
o.w: AWS Config records configuration state and compliance of existing resources for auditing purposes; it is not a provisioning or deployment tool and cannot create new infrastructure from the prototype.

o.t: Use AWS Systems Manager to replicate and provision the prototype infrastructure in two Availability Zones
o.w: AWS Systems Manager is primarily an operations and management tool for existing instances (patching, automation documents, inventory); it is not designed to replicate a full stack of resources like CloudFormation is.

o.t: Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk and configure it to use an automated reference to the prototype infrastructure to automatically deploy new environments in two Availability Zones.
o.w: Elastic Beanstalk manages application deployment on a predefined environment model, but it has no built-in feature that automatically reverse-engineers and replicates an existing manually-built set of resources.

explain: AWS CloudFormation is a service specifically designed for defining and deploying AWS infrastructure as code using templates. In this case, you can create a CloudFormation template based on the validated prototype infrastructure, and then use CloudFormation to deploy and manage the infrastructure in an automated and repeatable way.

q: A development team needs to host a website that will be accessed by other teams. The website contents consist of HTML, CSS, client-side JavaScript, and images. Which method is the MOST cost-effective for hosting the website?

o.t: Containerize the website and host it in AWS Fargate.
o.w: AWS Fargate runs containers and bills for compute time; it adds unnecessary cost and operational complexity for content that is purely static HTML/CSS/JS with no server-side processing.

o.t: Create an Amazon S3 bucket and host the website there.
o.w: Amazon S3 static website hosting serves HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images directly to browsers with no servers to provision or manage, making it the cheapest option for purely static content.

o.t: Deploy a web server on an Amazon EC2 instance to host the website.
o.w: Running a web server on an EC2 instance incurs continuous compute costs and patching/management overhead that are unnecessary for serving static files.

o.t: Configure an Application Load Balancer with an AWS Lambda target that uses the Express.js framework.
o.w: Express.js running on Lambda behind an ALB is designed for dynamic server-side applications and is far more complex and costly than needed for simple static content delivery.

explain:
Explanation:
The website is a static website because it consists only of HTML, CSS, client-side JavaScript, and images. The most cost-effective method is to create an Amazon S3 bucket and host the website there.

Amazon S3 is a highly scalable and cost-effective object storage service. It is suitable for hosting static websites because no web servers, containers, or backend compute resources are required.

To host the website on Amazon S3, the development team would create an S3 bucket, upload the website files to the bucket, and configure the bucket for static website hosting.

Option A is incorrect because AWS Fargate is used to run containers and is unnecessary for a static website. Option C is incorrect because an EC2 web server would add compute cost and operational overhead. Option D is incorrect because using an Application Load Balancer with Lambda and Express.js is overly complex for static content.

q: A solutions architect is designing a security solution for a company that wants to provide developers with individual AWS accounts through AWS Organizations, while also maintaining standard security controls. Because the individual developers will have AWS account root user-level access to their own accounts, the solutions architect wants to ensure that the mandatory AWS CloudTrail configuration that is applied to new developer accounts is not modified. Which action meets these requirements?

o.t: Create a new trail in CloudTrail from within the developer accounts with the organization trails option enabled.
o.w: Developers have root-user access in their own accounts, so they could delete or modify any trail they create themselves from within that account; an IAM-level control inside the account cannot restrain the root user.

o.t: Create a service-linked role for CloudTrail with a policy condition that allows changes only from an Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in the management account.
o.w: A service-linked role's policy conditions cannot override or block an AWS account root user's inherent permissions to modify or delete CloudTrail configuration within that same account.

o.t: Create a service control policy (SCP) that prohibits changes to CloudTrail, and attach it the developer accounts.
o.w: A service control policy (SCP) is enforced at the AWS Organizations level above the account, so it restricts even the root user's ability to change CloudTrail settings in member developer accounts, which is exactly what's needed here.

o.t: Create an IAM policy that prohibits changes to CloudTrail. and attach it to the root user.
o.w: IAM policies cannot be attached to or restrict the account root user; the root user bypasses IAM policy restrictions, so this would not actually prevent CloudTrail changes.

explain:
SCPs are used in AWS Organizations to set fine-grained permissions and restrictions on AWS accounts within the organization.
By creating an SCP that explicitly prohibits changes to CloudTrail settings, you can enforce this restriction across all developer accounts.

q: A company is implementing a shared storage solution for a gaming application that is hosted in the AWS Cloud. The company needs the ability to use Lustre clients to access data. The solution must be fully managed. Which solution meets these requirements?

o.t: Create an AWS DataSync task that shares the data as a mountable file system. Mount the file system to the application server.
o.w: AWS DataSync is a data transfer service for moving data between storage systems; it does not expose a Lustre-compatible mountable file system for applications to use as shared storage.

o.t: Create an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway. Create a file share that uses the required client protocol. Connect the application server to the file share.
o.w: Storage Gateway file gateway presents an NFS or SMB interface backed by S3, not a Lustre interface, so it cannot satisfy the requirement for native Lustre client access.

o.t: Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.
o.w: Amazon FSx for Lustre is a fully managed, native Lustre file system purpose-built for high-performance, concurrently-accessed shared storage, directly meeting both the Lustre-client and fully-managed requirements.

o.t: Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system, and configure it to support Lustre. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.
o.w: Amazon EFS is an NFS-based file system and has no mode or configuration to present a Lustre protocol interface; it cannot be made Lustre-compatible.

explain:
Amazon FSx for Lustre: Amazon FSx for Lustre is a fully managed service that provides high-performance shared storage. It is specifically designed to be used with Lustre, making it a suitable solution for Lustre clients.

Fully Managed: Amazon FSx for Lustre is a fully managed service, meaning that AWS takes care of maintenance, updates, and other operational tasks, reducing the management overhead for the company.

q: A company hosts a three-tier web application on Amazon EC2 instances in a single Availability Zone. The web application uses a self-managed MySQL database that is hosted on an EC2 instance to store data in an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. The MySQL database currently uses a 1 TB Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) EBS volume. The company expects traffic of 1,000 IOPS for both reads and writes at peak traffic. The company wants to minimize any disruptions, stabilize performance, and reduce costs while retaining the capacity for double the IOPS. The company wants to move the database tier to a fully managed solution that is highly available and fault tolerant. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

o.t: Use a Multi-AZ deployment of an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with an io2 Block Express EBS volume.
o.w: io2 Block Express provides very high provisioned IOPS performance but at a significantly higher cost than needed; since the workload only needs roughly double the current 1,000 IOPS, this is overkill and not the most cost-effective choice.

o.t: Use a Multi-AZ deployment of an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with a General Purpose SSD (gp2) EBS volume.
o.w: A Multi-AZ RDS for MySQL instance with a General Purpose SSD (gp2) volume is fully managed and highly available, and gp2 can provide burstable IOPS proportional to volume size that comfortably covers roughly double the current 1,000 IOPS requirement at a lower cost than Provisioned IOPS storage.

o.t: Use Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering access tiers.
o.w: Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering is an object storage class for infrequently accessed files; it is not a relational database engine and cannot replace a MySQL database tier.

o.t: Use two large EC2 instances to host the database in active-passive mode.
o.w: Manually running two EC2 instances in active-passive mode requires the company to self-manage failover, patching, and replication, which is not a fully managed solution and adds significant operational overhead and cost.

q: A company runs an application on a group of Amazon Linux EC2 instances. For compliance reasons, the company must retain all application log files for 7 years. The log files will be analyzed by a reporting tool that must be able to access all the files concurrently. Which storage solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

o.t: Amazon S3
o.w: Amazon S3 offers extremely low-cost, durable, long-term storage and natively supports many concurrent readers accessing the same objects, satisfying both the 7-year retention and concurrent-access requirements cost-effectively.

o.t: Amazon EC2 instance store
o.w: EC2 instance store is ephemeral storage tied to the life of the instance; data is lost when the instance stops or terminates, making it unsuitable for 7-year compliance retention.

o.t: Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
o.w: Amazon EBS volumes attach to a single EC2 instance and are not designed for being concurrently read by multiple separate processes/tools, and long-term EBS storage is costlier than S3 for archival-style logs.

o.t: Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS)
o.w: Amazon EFS supports concurrent access and could technically work, but its per-GB cost is notably higher than S3 for long-term, large-scale log storage, making it less cost-effective for a 7-year retention requirement.

explain: S3 is a highly durable and scalable object storage service. It is designed for high availability and can store large amounts of data. S3 is cost-effective for long-term storage, and its pricing is based on the amount of data stored.

q: A company is deploying a new application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application writes data to Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes. The company needs to ensure that all data that is written to the EBS volumes is encrypted at rest. Which solution will meet this requirement?

o.t: Create an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key policy that enforces EBS encryption in the account. Ensure that the key policy is active.
o.w: A KMS key policy governs who can use a key; it does not force EBS volumes to be created as encrypted, volumes could still be created unencrypted regardless of key policy settings.

o.t: Create an EC2 instance tag that has a key of Encrypt and a value of True. Tag all instances that require encryption at the EBS level.
o.w: EC2 tags are purely metadata for organization and automation triggers; a tag by itself does not cause Amazon EBS to actually encrypt a volume.

o.t: Create the EBS volumes as encrypted volumes. Attach the EBS volumes to the EC2 instances.
o.w: Explicitly creating EBS volumes with encryption enabled ensures that all data written to those volumes is automatically encrypted at rest using AWS-managed encryption under the hood.

o.t: Create an IAM role that specifies EBS encryption. Attach the role to the EC2 instances.
o.w: IAM roles grant permissions to call AWS APIs; there is no IAM role setting that directly causes an EBS volume to be encrypted, the encryption flag must be set at volume creation (or via default EBS encryption).

explain: By creating the EBS volumes as encrypted volumes, you ensure that all data written to those volumes is automatically encrypted. This provides a straightforward and effective solution for meeting the encryption-at-rest requirement.

q: A company has several on-premises Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (ISCSI) network storage servers. The company wants to reduce the number of these servers by moving to the AWS Cloud. A solutions architect must provide low-latency access to frequently used data and reduce the dependency on on-premises servers with a minimal number of infrastructure changes. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Deploy Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage with backups to Amazon S3.
o.w: Amazon EBS is cloud-native block storage attached to EC2 instances; it does not integrate with on-premises iSCSI initiators and does not reduce dependency on existing on-premises storage servers with minimal changes.

o.t: Deploy an Amazon S3 File Gateway.
o.w: An S3 File Gateway presents an NFS/SMB file interface, not the iSCSI block interface the on-premises applications currently use, so it would require significant application changes rather than a minimal-change migration.

o.t: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway that is configured with stored volumes.
o.w: Stored volumes keep the primary copy of data on-premises and only asynchronously back it up to S3, so they do not reduce the number of on-premises storage servers needed, failing the goal of reducing on-premises dependency.

o.t: Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway that is configured with cached volumes.
o.w: Cached volumes present an iSCSI interface matching existing clients with minimal changes, store the full dataset durably in Amazon S3, and keep only frequently accessed data cached locally for low latency, directly meeting all stated requirements.

explain: A volume gateway with cached volumes is a good fit when you want to keep frequently accessed data on-premises for low-latency access while still having a copy in the AWS Cloud. Cached volumes store the entire dataset in Amazon S3 while retaining the most frequently accessed data locally.

q: A company moved its on-premises PostgreSQL database to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The company successfully launched a new product. The workload on the database has increased. The company wants to accommodate the larger workload without adding infrastructure. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

o.t: Buy reserved DB instances for the total workload. Make the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance larger.
o.w: Resizing the existing RDS instance to a larger instance class increases its compute/memory capacity to handle the larger workload without adding a new piece of infrastructure, and purchasing Reserved Instances for that capacity reduces the ongoing cost compared to On-Demand pricing.

o.t: Make the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance a Multi-AZ DB instance.
o.w: Enabling Multi-AZ adds a standby replica for availability and failover, but it does not increase the primary instance's compute capacity to handle a higher workload.

o.t: Buy reserved DB instances for the total workload. Add another Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance.
o.w: Adding another separate RDS DB instance increases the number of infrastructure components, directly violating the requirement to accommodate the workload without adding infrastructure.

o.t: Make the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance an on-demand DB instance.
o.w: Switching to (or remaining on) an On-Demand instance costs more per hour over a sustained period than a Reserved Instance, making it the less cost-effective option for predictable, continuous workloads.

explain:
When you commit to using a database instance for a longer time (with reserved instances), AWS gives you a discount compared to paying on a month-to-month basis.

Imagine you have a computer, and you want to make it more powerful because you have more things to do on it. Making the instance larger means upgrading the power of your virtual computer.

q: A research laboratory needs to process approximately 8 TB of data. The laboratory requires sub-millisecond latencies and a minimum throughput of 6 GBps for the storage subsystem. Hundreds of Amazon EC2 instances that run Amazon Linux will distribute and process the data. Which solution will meet the performance requirements?

o.t: Create an Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file system. Sat each volume’ tiering policy to ALL. Import the raw data into the file system. Mount the fila system on the EC2 instances.
o.w: Setting the tiering policy to ALL moves cold data out to lower-performance capacity storage, which undermines consistent sub-millisecond latency, and FSx for ONTAP's architecture is not optimized for this kind of raw high-throughput HPC workload compared to Lustre.

o.t: Create an Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file system. Set each volume’s tiering policy to NONE. Import the raw data into the file system. Mount the file system on the EC2 instances.
o.w: Even with tiering disabled, Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP is designed for general-purpose enterprise file workloads rather than the sub-millisecond, massively parallel throughput needs of an HPC compute cluster, which Lustre specifically targets.

o.t: Create an Amazon S3 bucket to store the raw data. Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system that uses persistent HDD storage. Select the option to import data from and export data to Amazon S3. Mount the file system on the EC2 instances.
o.w: Persistent HDD storage for FSx for Lustre is optimized for lower-cost, throughput-oriented workloads but cannot reliably deliver the required 6 GBps combined with sub-millisecond latency the way SSD-backed storage can.

o.t: Create an Amazon S3 bucket to store the raw data. Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system that uses persistent SSD storage. Select the option to import data from and export data to Amazon S3. Mount the file system on the EC2 instances.
o.w: FSx for Lustre with persistent SSD storage is purpose-built for high-performance computing, delivering sub-millisecond latencies and very high throughput, and its native S3 data repository integration lets hundreds of compute instances import/export data from the 8 TB S3 dataset seamlessly.

explain:
Amazon FSx for Lustre is a high-performance file system designed for use with compute-intensive workloads. It provides sub-millisecond latencies and is well-suited for scenarios where high throughput is required.
Using persistent SSD storage for the Amazon FSx for Lustre file system ensures that it meets the minimum throughput requirement of 6 GBps.
Storing the raw data in an Amazon S3 bucket allows for scalable and durable storage, and the integration with FSx for Lustre allows seamless importing and exporting of data to and from S3.
This solution is designed to provide the required performance characteristics for processing large amounts of data with hundreds of EC2 instances.

q: An ecommerce company runs an application in the AWS Cloud that is integrated with an on-premises warehouse solution. The company uses Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to send order messages to an on-premises HTTPS endpoint so the warehouse application can process the orders. The local data center team has detected that some of the order messages were not received. A solutions architect needs to retain messages that are not delivered and analyze the messages for up to 14 days. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

o.t: Add an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue with a retention period of 14 days between the application and Amazon SNS.
o.w: Placing an SQS queue upstream of SNS between the application and SNS does not address the problem: SNS itself is still delivering directly to the flaky on-premises HTTPS endpoint, and failed deliveries to that endpoint are not captured by this queue.

o.t: Configure an Amazon SNS dead letter queue that has an Amazon DynamoDB target with a TTL attribute set for a retention period of 14 days.
o.w: Using DynamoDB as the dead-letter target requires designing a table schema and writing custom logic to analyze the failed messages, which is more development effort than simply using a native SQS dead-letter queue for retention and inspection.

o.t: Configure an Amazon SNS dead letter queue that has an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream target with a retention period of 14 days.
o.w: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams requires setting up shards, consumers, and custom processing logic to read and analyze records, representing considerably more development effort than directly using SQS as the DLQ target.

o.t: Configure an Amazon SNS dead letter queue that has an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) target with a retention period of 14 days.
o.w: Amazon SNS supports configuring a dead-letter queue directly on a subscription, and an SQS queue naturally retains undelivered messages for a configurable period up to 14 days, letting the security/ops team inspect them with no custom development.

explain:
Amazon SNS allows you to set up a dead letter queue to capture and retain messages that cannot be delivered to the intended endpoint.
When configuring a DLQ, you can specify an Amazon SQS queue as the target for messages that fail to be delivered.
Amazon SQS provides message retention settings, and in this case, you can set the retention period to 14 days.

q: A company needs to migrate a legacy application from an on-premises data center to the AWS Cloud because of hardware capacity constraints. The application runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. The application’s database storage continues to grow over time. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

o.t: Migrate the application layer to Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances. Migrate the data storage layer to Amazon RDS On-Demand Instances.
o.w: Running the RDS database on On-Demand pricing for a workload that runs continuously 24/7 forfeits the substantial discount that Reserved Instances would provide for that steady-state usage.

o.t: Migrate the application layer to Amazon EC2 Spot Instances. Migrate the data storage layer to Amazon S3.
o.w: Spot Instances can be interrupted with little notice, which is unsuitable for a legacy application that must run continuously 24/7, and Amazon S3 is object storage, not a relational database engine that can replace the application's database tier.

o.t: Migrate the application layer to Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances. Migrate the data storage layer to Amazon Aurora Reserved Instances.
o.w: Using Reserved Instances for both the always-on EC2 application layer and the Aurora database layer captures the maximum discount for predictable, continuous 24/7 usage, while Aurora's managed, scalable storage handles the database's ongoing growth efficiently.

o.t: Migrate the application layer to Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances. Migrate the data storage layer to Amazon RDS Reserved Instances.
o.w: Running the EC2 application layer On-Demand for a workload that runs continuously 24/7 misses out on the Reserved Instance discount that would apply to that steady, predictable usage.

explain:
Using Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances for the application layer provides cost savings compared to On-Demand Instances while ensuring availability for the 24/7 runtime.
Migrating the data storage layer to Amazon Aurora Reserved Instances provides a fully managed relational database service with automatic scaling capabilities. Amazon Aurora is designed for high performance and cost efficiency.
Reserved Instances provide cost savings compared to On-Demand Instances over an extended period, making them suitable for applications with continuous operation.
Amazon Aurora, being a fully managed service, offloads much of the operational overhead associated with managing a traditional database, making it a cost-effective choice for growing database storage.

q: A company is building a data analysis platform on AWS by using AWS Lake Formation. The platform will ingest data from different sources such as Amazon S3 and Amazon RDS. The company needs a secure solution to prevent access to portions of the data that contain sensitive information. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

o.t: Create an AWS Lambda function that periodically queries and removes sensitive information from Lake Formation tables.
o.w: A custom Lambda function that periodically scans and strips sensitive data requires ongoing development, scheduling, and maintenance, which is significantly more operational overhead than using Lake Formation's built-in fine-grained access controls.

o.t: Create data filters to implement row-level security and cell-level security.
o.w: Lake Formation data filters let administrators declaratively restrict specific rows and columns containing sensitive data per principal, without writing or maintaining any custom code, directly satisfying the requirement with minimal operational overhead.

o.t: Create an IAM role that includes permissions to access Lake Formation tables.
o.w: An IAM role granting table-level access controls whether a principal can access a table at all, but it cannot selectively hide specific sensitive rows or columns within that table.

o.t: Create an AWS Lambda function that removes sensitive information before Lake Formation ingests the data.
o.w: Stripping sensitive data before ingestion would also remove it for the one application that legitimately needs to process the PII, and maintaining a custom pre-ingestion Lambda adds ongoing operational overhead that native data filters avoid.

explain: AWS Lake Formation allows you to create data filters that can be used for row-level security and cell-level security.

q: A law firm needs to share information with the public. The information includes hundreds of files that must be publicly readable. Modifications or deletions of the files by anyone before a designated future date are prohibited. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way?

o.t: Create a new Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Versioning enabled. Use S3 Object Lock with a retention period in accordance with the designated date. Configure the S3 bucket for static website hosting. Set an S3 bucket policy to allow read-only access to the objects.
o.w: S3 Object Lock, which requires Versioning, can enforce a retention period that even the bucket owner and root user cannot override, so combined with a read-only bucket policy for public access, this guarantees the files truly cannot be modified or deleted before the designated date.

o.t: Upload all files to an Amazon S3 bucket that is configured for static website hosting. Grant read-only IAM permissions to any AWS principals that access the S3 bucket until the designated date.
o.w: Granting read-only IAM permissions to principals can be changed or revoked at any time by an administrator; it is a reversible access control, not an enforced retention lock, so it does not truly prohibit modification or deletion the way Object Lock does.

o.t: Upload all files to an Amazon S3 bucket that is configured for static website hosting. Select the folder that contains the files. Use S3 Object Lock with a retention period in accordance with the designated date. Grant read-only IAM permissions to any AWS principals that access the S3 bucket.
o.w: Selecting a folder to apply Object Lock to after upload is not how S3 Object Lock works, retention must be set per object, and relying on IAM permissions alone is still reversible by an administrator.

o.t: Create a new Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Versioning enabled. Configure an event trigger to run an AWS Lambda function in case of object modification or deletion. Configure the Lambda function to replace the objects with the original versions from a private S3 bucket.
o.w: This approach is reactive, not preventive: it only restores objects after they have already been modified or deleted, so there is a window where distribution rights could be violated, and the Lambda automation itself adds unnecessary complexity.

explain: S3 Versioning helps maintain multiple versions of an object over time. With S3 Object Lock, you can enforce retention periods during which the objects cannot be modified or deleted. This aligns with the requirement to prohibit modifications or deletions before a designated future date.

q: A company needs to provide its employees with secure access to confidential and sensitive files. The company wants to ensure that the files can be accessed only by authorized users. The files must be downloaded securely to the employees’ devices. The files are stored in an on-premises Windows file server. However, due to an increase in remote usage, the file server is running out of capacity. . Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Migrate the files to Amazon S3, and create a public VPC endpoint. Allow employees to sign on with AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On).
o.w: A VPC endpoint is a private connectivity construct, not something you make 'public,' and migrating to plain S3 abandons the existing Windows file share permissions model, requiring a redesign of how access control is enforced for employees.

o.t: Migrate the file server to an Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet. Configure the security group to limit inbound traffic to the employees’ IP addresses.
o.w: Simply lifting the file server onto an EC2 instance in a public subnet exposes it directly to the internet and still leaves a single, non-redundant server with the same capacity constraints, rather than a scalable, more secure managed solution.

o.t: Migrate the files to an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. Integrate the Amazon FSx file system with the on-premises Active Directory. Configure AWS Client VPN.
o.w: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server integrated with the existing on-premises Active Directory preserves familiar file permissions, offloads capacity concerns to a fully managed, scalable service, and AWS Client VPN gives employees secure, authenticated remote access to download files.

o.t: Migrate the files to Amazon S3, and create a private VPC endpoint. Create a signed URL to allow download.
o.w: Amazon S3 does not natively replicate Windows file-share semantics (ACLs, SMB), and signed URLs would need to be generated and distributed individually, which doesn't cleanly replace a file-server-based access model for all employees.

explain:
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server: It is a fully managed file storage service built on Windows Server. It is designed to be integrated with on-premises Active Directory, allowing for a seamless extension of your existing directory and authentication infrastructure to the AWS Cloud.

Integrate with On-Premises Active Directory: With Amazon FSx, you can integrate the file system with your on-premises Active Directory, ensuring that the same user accounts and permissions are used both on-premises and in the cloud.

q: An ecommerce company stores terabytes of customer data in the AWS Cloud. The data contains personally identifiable information (PII). The company wants to use the data in three applications. Only one of the applications needs to process the PII. The PII must be removed before the other two applications process the data. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

o.t: Process the data and store the transformed data in three separate Amazon DynamoDB tables so that each application has its own custom dataset. Point each application to its respective DynamoDB table.
o.w: Pre-processing and duplicating the dataset into three separate DynamoDB tables means building and maintaining three ETL pipelines and three copies of the data, which is far more operational overhead than transforming data on the fly.

o.t: Process the data and store the transformed data in three separate Amazon S3 buckets so that each application has its own custom dataset. Point each application to its respective S3 bucket.
o.w: Creating three separate S3 buckets with their own pre-transformed copies of the data requires ongoing synchronization and duplicate storage, adding operational overhead compared to serving a single source of truth with on-the-fly transformation.

o.t: Store the data in an Amazon S3 bucket. Process and transform the data by using S3 Object Lambda before returning the data to the requesting application.
o.w: S3 Object Lambda lets you attach a Lambda function to GET requests on a single copy of data in S3, dynamically stripping PII for the two applications that shouldn't see it while leaving the original object untouched for the one that needs it, avoiding any duplicate storage or pipelines.

o.t: Store the data in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Create a proxy application layer to intercept and process the data that each application requests.
o.w: Building a custom proxy application layer to intercept and filter DynamoDB requests requires developing and operating new middleware, which is considerably more operational overhead than using the managed S3 Object Lambda feature.

explain:
S3 Object Lambda allows you to add custom code to process and transform data as it is requested by applications, without having to modify the original data stored in S3.
By using S3 Object Lambda, you can process and remove the personally identifiable information (PII) on-the-fly before returning the data to the applications.
This approach minimizes operational overhead because you don't need to create separate storage (buckets or tables) for each application, and you can apply the PII removal logic dynamically as the data is requested.

q: A company has a three-tier application for image sharing. The application uses an Amazon EC2 instance for the front-end layer, another EC2 instance for the application layer, and a third EC2 instance for a MySQL database. A solutions architect must design a scalable and highly available solution that requires the least amount of change to the application. Which solution meets these requirements?

o.t: Use Amazon S3 to host the front-end layer. Use a fleet of EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group for the application layer. Move the database to a memory optimized instance type to store and serve users’ images.
o.w: Simply moving the database to a larger, memory-optimized EC2 instance still leaves it as a single, self-managed instance with no automatic failover, so it does not achieve true high availability for the database tier.

o.t: Use load-balanced Multi-AZ AWS Elastic Beanstalk environments for the front-end layer and the application layer. Move the database to an Amazon RDS DB instance with multiple read replicas to serve users’ images.
o.w: Read replicas improve read scalability but do not provide an automatic failover for the writer if the primary instance or its Availability Zone fails, so this does not deliver full high availability for the database tier.

o.t: Use load-balanced Multi-AZ AWS Elastic Beanstalk environments for the front-end layer and the application layer. Move the database to an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance. Use Amazon S3 to store and serve users’ images.
o.w: Load-balanced Multi-AZ Elastic Beanstalk environments give the front-end and application tiers automatic scaling and AZ-level redundancy, an RDS Multi-AZ instance gives the database tier automatic failover, and offloading images to S3 removes a scaling bottleneck, achieving HA and scalability with minimal application rewrite.

o.t: Use Amazon S3 to host the front-end layer. Use AWS Lambda functions for the application layer. Move the database to an Amazon DynamoDB table. Use Amazon S3 to store and serve users’ images.
o.w: Rewriting the application layer to run as AWS Lambda functions and migrating the relational schema to DynamoDB is a major application redesign, violating the requirement for the least amount of change to the application.

explain:
AWS Elastic Beanstalk provides an easy way to deploy and manage applications. By using Multi-AZ environments, the front-end and application layers can automatically scale and provide high availability across multiple Availability Zones (AZs).
Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB Instance:
Moving the database to an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance ensures high availability and automatic failover in the event of a failure in one Availability Zone.
Amazon S3 for Storing and Serving Images:
Using Amazon S3 for storing and serving users' images is a scalable and cost-effective solution. S3 is designed for high durability and availability, making it suitable for serving static content like images.

q: A solutions architect is designing the architecture of a new application being deployed to the AWS Cloud. The application will run on Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances and will automatically scale across multiple Availability Zones. The EC2 instances will scale up and down frequently throughout the day. An Application Load Balancer (ALB) will handle the load distribution. The architecture needs to support distributed session data management. The company is willing to make changes to code if needed. What should the solutions architect do to ensure that the architecture supports distributed session data management?

o.t: Use Amazon ElastiCache to manage and store session data.
o.w: Amazon ElastiCache provides a fast, shared, external data store that any EC2 instance behind the ALB can read/write session data from, so sessions remain available regardless of which instance (or how many) are currently running, a true distributed session management solution.

o.t: Use Session Manager from AWS Systems Manager to manage the session.
o.w: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager is a tool for establishing secure shell/remote access sessions to manage instances; it has nothing to do with storing a web application's user session data.

o.t: Use the GetSessionToken API operation in AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) to manage the session.
o.w: AWS STS GetSessionToken issues temporary AWS credentials for API access; it is unrelated to managing a web application's user session state.

o.t: Use session affinity (sticky sessions) of the ALB to manage session data.
o.w: Sticky sessions pin a user's session to one specific instance, which breaks down when that instance is terminated during scale-in, meaning session data is not actually distributed or resilient to scaling events.

explain:
Amazon ElastiCache is a fully managed, in-memory data store service. It is commonly used for caching and session management in distributed applications.
By utilizing ElastiCache for session data management, you can store and retrieve session data in a scalable and high-performance manner.
The use of ElastiCache allows for a distributed and shared data store for session management across multiple instances and Availability Zones.

q: A company runs its applications on both Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) clusters and on-premises Kubernetes clusters. The company wants to view all clusters and workloads from a central location. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

o.t: Use AWS Systems Manager to collect and view the cluster information.
o.w: AWS Systems Manager is designed for managing EC2 instances and on-premises servers/VMs; it does not natively discover or display Kubernetes cluster and workload inventory.

o.t: Use Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights to collect and group the cluster information.
o.w: CloudWatch Container Insights collects performance metrics and logs from clusters it's configured to monitor, but it isn't designed to connect and centrally register unmanaged on-premises Kubernetes clusters alongside EKS clusters in one unified console view.

o.t: Use Amazon EKS Anywhere as the primary cluster to view the other clusters with native Kubernetes commands.
o.w: Treating one EKS Anywhere cluster as a 'primary' and using native kubectl commands to view other clusters requires manually managing kubeconfigs and contexts for every cluster, this is not a centralized, low-overhead viewing solution.

o.t: Use Amazon EKS Connector to register and connect all Kubernetes clusters.
o.w: Amazon EKS Connector is purpose-built to register both EKS and non-EKS (including on-premises) Kubernetes clusters so they all appear and can be viewed together in the EKS console, meeting the central-visibility requirement with minimal setup.

explain: Amazon EKS Connector is designed to help centralize the management of multiple Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) clusters. It allows you to register and connect multiple EKS clusters, providing a unified view of the clusters from the AWS Management Console. This solution aligns well with the requirement of managing clusters and workloads from a central location with the least operational overhead.

q: A global marketing company has applications that run in the ap-southeast-2 Region and the eu-west-1 Region. Applications that run in a VPC in euwest-1 need to communicate securely with databases that run in a VPC in ap-southeast-2. Which network design will meet these requirements?

o.t: Create a VPC peering connection between the eu-west-1 VPC and the ap-southeast-2 VPC. Create an inbound rule in the eu-west-1 application security group that allows traffic from the database server IP addresses in the ap-southeast-2 security group.
o.w: This rule is on the wrong side and in the wrong direction, the eu-west-1 application security group doesn't need an inbound rule allowing traffic from database IPs; it's the database's security group in ap-southeast-2 that needs to allow inbound traffic from the application servers.

o.t: Create a transit gateway with a peering attachment between the eu-west-1 VPC and the ap-southeast-2 VPC. After the transit gateways are properly peered and routing is configured, create an inbound rule in the database security group that references the security group ID of the application servers in eu-west-1.
o.w: With an inter-Region Transit Gateway peering attachment, security group rules cannot directly reference a security group ID from a peered VPC in a different Region, only CIDR-based rules are supported across Regions, so this configuration would not work as described.

o.t: Configure a VPC peering connection between the ap-southeast-2 VPC and the eu-west-1 VPUpdate the subnet route tables. Create an inbound rule in the ap-southeast-2 database security group that allows traffic from the eu-west-1 application server IP addresses.
o.w: A VPC peering connection between the two Regions, correctly updated route tables, and an inbound rule on the ap-southeast-2 database security group that allows traffic from the eu-west-1 application servers' IP address ranges is exactly how secure communication is established for cross-Region VPC peering, since cross-Region peering only supports CIDR-based security group rules.

o.t: Configure a VPC peering connection between the ap-southeast-2 VPC and the eu-west-1 VPC. Update the subnet route tables. Create an inbound rule in the ap-southeast-2 database security group that references the security group ID of the application servers in eu-west-1.
o.w: Amazon VPC peering connections between two different AWS Regions do not support referencing a security group ID from the peer VPC in security group rules, only IP address (CIDR)-based rules are supported for inter-Region peering, so this rule would fail to function as intended.

explain:
VPC peering connections can be established between VPCs in different AWS Regions.
In this case, a VPC peering connection is set up between the VPC in ap-southeast-2 and the VPC in eu-west-1.

q: A company is relocating its data center and wants to securely transfer 50 TB of data to AWS within 2 weeks. The existing data center has a Site-toSite VPN connection to AWS that is 90% utilized. Which AWS service should a solutions architect use to meet these requirements?

o.t: AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized
o.w: AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized is a physical device that can hold tens of terabytes of data and ships via courier, bypassing the nearly saturated network link entirely, it reliably moves 50 TB within a 2-week window regardless of available bandwidth.

o.t: AWS Storage Gateway
o.w: AWS Storage Gateway is designed for ongoing hybrid cloud storage integration over an existing network connection; it still depends on available network bandwidth, which is already 90% utilized, making it unsuitable for a one-time bulk transfer under a tight deadline.

o.t: AWS Direct Connect
o.w: Provisioning a new AWS Direct Connect connection typically takes weeks to months to establish, which would not meet the 2-week transfer deadline.

o.t: AWS DataSync with a VPC endpoint
o.w: AWS DataSync still transfers data over the existing network link (even via a VPC endpoint), so with the Site-to-Site VPN already at 90% utilization, there isn't enough remaining bandwidth to move 50 TB in the required timeframe.

q: A company runs a fleet of web servers using an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. After a routine compliance check, the company sets a standard that requires a recovery point objective (RPO) of less than 1 second for all its production databases. Which solution meets these requirements?

o.t: Configure the DB instance in one Availability Zone, and create multiple read replicas in a separate Availability Zone.
o.w: Read replicas use asynchronous replication, which can lag behind the primary by more than a second under load, and there's no automatic failover to a read replica, so this doesn't reliably guarantee an RPO under 1 second.

o.t: Enable a Multi-AZ deployment for the DB instance.
o.w: Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployments use synchronous replication to a standby in another AZ, so committed transactions are durably copied before being acknowledged, giving an RPO at or near zero (sub-second) and automatic failover if the primary fails.

o.t: Enable auto scaling for the DB instance in one Availability Zone.
o.w: Auto scaling adjusts compute/storage capacity for a single-AZ instance; it has nothing to do with replicating data to protect against data loss, so it does not address the RPO requirement at all.

o.t: Configure the DB instance in one Availability Zone, and configure AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) change data capture (CDC) tasks.
o.w: AWS DMS change data capture replicates changes to a target, but it operates asynchronously and is intended for migration/replication pipelines, not for providing a guaranteed sub-second RPO with automatic failover like Multi-AZ synchronous replication does.

explain: A Multi-AZ (Availability Zone) deployment for Amazon RDS provides high availability and failover support for DB instances. In a Multi-AZ deployment, Amazon RDS automatically provisions and maintains a synchronous standby replica in a different Availability Zone.

q: A solutions architect observes that a nightly batch processing job is automatically scaled up for 1 hour before the desired Amazon EC2 capacity is reached. The peak capacity is the ‘same every night and the batch jobs always start at 1 AM. The solutions architect needs to find a cost-effective solution that will allow for the desired EC2 capacity to be reached quickly and allow the Auto Scaling group to scale down after the batch jobs are complete. What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

o.t: Configure scheduled scaling to scale up to the desired compute level.
o.w: Scheduled scaling lets you set the desired/min/max capacity to the known peak values at a specific time shortly before 1 AM and then revert afterward, so the fleet is already at full size when the predictable nightly job starts, and it scales back down afterward without wasting cost the rest of the day.

o.t: Increase the maximum capacity for the Auto Scaling group.
o.w: Raising the maximum capacity only raises the ceiling the Auto Scaling group is allowed to reach; it does not change how quickly or when the scaling actually happens, so the 1-hour ramp-up delay before the nightly job would still occur.

o.t: Change the scaling policy to add more EC2 instances during each scaling operation.
o.w: Adding more instances per scaling step still relies on reactive dynamic/step scaling triggered by a metric crossing a threshold after the job already starts, so it does not guarantee capacity is ready at 1 AM, and it has no built-in scale-down after the predictable job window.

o.t: Increase the minimum capacity for the Auto Scaling group.
o.w: Increasing the minimum capacity keeps that many instances running around the clock even outside the nightly batch window, which wastes money, failing the cost-effectiveness requirement.

explain:
Scheduled scaling allows you to define specific times when your Auto Scaling group's desired capacity should be increased or decreased.
In this case, you can schedule the scaling action to increase the capacity just before the nightly batch processing job starts at 1 AM and then scale it down after the job completes.

q: A company has an AWS Lambda function that needs read access to an Amazon S3 bucket that is located in the same AWS account. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure manner?

o.t: Embed an access key and a secret key in the Lambda function’s code to grant the required IAM permissions for read access to the S3 bucket.
o.w: Embedding long-lived access keys directly in code is a major security anti-pattern, keys can leak through source control or logs, and Lambda already has a built-in, more secure way to obtain temporary credentials via an execution role.

o.t: Apply an IAM role to the Lambda function. Apply an IAM policy to the role to grant read access to all S3 buckets in the account.
o.w: Granting read access to all S3 buckets in the account violates the principle of least privilege; if the function or its role is ever compromised, the blast radius extends to every bucket in the account rather than just the one it actually needs.

o.t: Apply an IAM role to the Lambda function. Apply an IAM policy to the role to grant read access to the S3 bucket.
o.w: Attaching an IAM execution role to the Lambda function with a policy scoped to read-only access on just the specific required S3 bucket follows least privilege, uses temporary credentials automatically managed by Lambda, and minimizes the impact of any compromise.

o.t: Apply an S3 bucket policy that grants read access to the S3 bucket.
o.w: A bucket policy alone, without a corresponding IAM identity-based permission for the Lambda execution role, is a less standard and less tightly scoped approach; the straightforward and best-practice method is an IAM role/policy on the function.

explain:
An IAM role provides temporary credentials to the Lambda function to access AWS resources. The function does not have persistent credentials.
The IAM policy grants least privilege access by specifying read access only to the specific S3 bucket needed. Access is not granted to all S3 buckets.
If the Lambda function is compromised, the attacker would only gain access to the one specified S3 bucket. They would not receive broad access to resources.

q: A company is building an application in the AWS Cloud. The application will store data in Amazon S3 buckets in two AWS Regions. The company must use an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key to encrypt all data that is stored in the S3 buckets. The data in both S3 buckets must be encrypted and decrypted with the same KMS key. The data and the key must be stored in each of the two Regions. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

o.t: Create a customer managed multi-Region KMS key. Create an S3 bucket in each Region. Configure replication between the S3 buckets. Configure the application to use the KMS key with client-side encryption.
o.w: An AWS KMS multi-Region key maintains the same key material under related key IDs in each Region, and since S3 replication doesn't transparently share a single customer managed key across Regions via server-side encryption, client-side encryption with the multi-Region key lets data be encrypted and decrypted with identical cryptographic material in either Region with minimal extra operational work.

o.t: Create a customer managed KMS key and an S3 bucket in each Region. Configure the S3 buckets to use server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). Configure replication between the S3 buckets.
o.w: Creating separate single-Region customer managed KMS keys in each Region means the data isn't actually protected by the same key, and S3 server-side encryption with KMS (SSE-KMS) does not transparently use one customer managed key across Regions for replicated data.

o.t: Create an S3 bucket in each Region. Configure the S3 buckets to use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Configure replication between the S3 buckets.
o.w: SSE-S3 uses Amazon S3-managed encryption keys, not an AWS KMS customer managed key at all, so it does not meet the explicit requirement to use a customer managed KMS key for encryption.

o.t: Create a customer managed KMS key and an S3 bucket in each Region. Configure the S3 buckets to use server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3). Configure replication between the S3 buckets.
o.w: Even though a customer managed KMS key is created, configuring the buckets to use SSE-S3 means S3 encrypts objects with S3-managed keys instead, so the KMS key created isn't actually being used to encrypt the data as required.

explain:
Explanation:
The requirement says that the data in both S3 buckets must be encrypted and decrypted with the same KMS key, and that the key must exist in both AWS Regions. This points to an AWS KMS multi-Region customer managed key. A multi-Region KMS key has related keys in different Regions with the same key material, which allows data encrypted in one Region to be decrypted in another Region.

Option A is incorrect because SSE-S3 uses Amazon S3 managed keys, not AWS KMS customer managed keys. Option C is incorrect because it creates customer managed KMS keys but then uses SSE-S3. Option D is close, but it creates separate KMS keys in each Region instead of using a multi-Region KMS key with the same key material.

q: A company is preparing to launch a public-facing web application in the AWS Cloud. The architecture consists of Amazon EC2 instances within a VPC behind an Elastic Load Balancer (ELB). A third-party service is used for the DNS. The company's solutions architect must recommend a solution to detect and protect against large-scale DDoS attacks. Which solution meets these requirements?

o.t: Enable Amazon GuardDuty on the account.
o.w: Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that analyzes logs for malicious activity and anomalies; it does not provide active DDoS mitigation capacity for load balancers.

o.t: Enable Amazon Inspector on the EC2 instances.
o.w: Amazon Inspector performs vulnerability and software composition scanning on workloads; it has no function related to detecting or mitigating large-scale DDoS attacks.

o.t: Enable AWS Shield and assign Amazon Route 53 to it.
o.w: AWS Shield Standard is automatically enabled and free for all AWS customers and doesn't need to be 'assigned,' and since the company uses a third-party DNS provider rather than Route 53, there's no AWS-hosted Route 53 resource to protect with Shield in this scenario.

o.t: Enable AWS Shield Advanced and assign the ELB to it.
o.w: AWS Shield Advanced provides enhanced, large-scale DDoS detection and mitigation and can be explicitly attached to resources like an Elastic Load Balancer, giving continuous protection and visibility specifically for the ELB handling the public-facing traffic.

explain: AWS Shield Advanced provides expanded DDoS attack protection for your Amazon EC2 instances, Elastic Load Balancing load balancers, CloudFront distributions, Route 53 hosted zones, and AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerators.

q: An Amazon EC2 instance is located in a private subnet in a new VPC. This subnet does not have outbound internet access, but the EC2 instance needs the ability to download monthly security updates from an outside vendor. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

o.t: Create an internet gateway, and attach it to the VPC. Create a NAT instance, and place it in the same subnet where the EC2 instance is located. Configure the private subnet route table to use the internet gateway as the default route.
o.w: This mixes up the routing: placing a NAT instance inside the private subnet it's meant to serve while routing that same private subnet's default traffic to the Internet Gateway directly would expose the subnet publicly and defeats the purpose of using a NAT instance at all.

o.t: Create a NAT instance, and place it in the same subnet where the EC2 instance is located. Configure the private subnet route table to use the NAT instance as the default route.
o.w: A NAT instance needs to live in a public subnet with its own route to an internet gateway to have internet access itself; placing it in the private subnet (with no route out) gives the NAT instance no way to reach the internet either.

o.t: Create an internet gateway, and attach it to the VPC. Configure the private subnet route table to use the internet gateway as the default route.
o.w: Routing the private subnet directly to an internet gateway effectively turns it into a public subnet, requiring instances to have public IP addresses to communicate out, this removes the privacy/security boundary the company wants to keep for this subnet.

o.t: Create a NAT gateway, and place it in a public subnet. Configure the private subnet route table to use the NAT gateway as the default route.
o.w: A NAT gateway placed in a public subnet (which does have a route to an internet gateway) lets instances in the private subnet initiate outbound connections like downloading updates, while still blocking unsolicited inbound connections from the internet, with no management overhead since it's a fully managed AWS service.

explain: NAT gateways are designed to provide outbound internet access for instances in private subnets. Placing a NAT gateway in a public subnet and configuring the private subnet's route table to use the NAT gateway as the default route allows the EC2 instance to download security updates while maintaining security.

q: A company needs to connect several VPCs in the us-east-1 Region that span hundreds of AWS accounts. The company's networking team has its own AWS account to manage the cloud network. What is the MOST operationally efficient solution to connect the VPCs?

o.t: Set up VPC peering connections between each VPC. Update each associated subnet’s route table
o.w: VPC peering connections are point-to-point and don't transitively route, so connecting hundreds of VPCs this way would require managing an enormous number of individual peering connections and route table entries, an unscalable operational burden.

o.t: Create an AWS Transit Gateway in the networking team’s AWS account. Configure static routes from each VPC.
o.w: AWS Transit Gateway acts as a single central hub that each VPC attaches to with one connection, letting the networking team manage routing centrally from their own account; this scales far more efficiently than a full mesh of individual connections for hundreds of VPCs.

o.t: Configure a NAT gateway and an internet gateway in each VPC to connect each VPC through the internet
o.w: Routing inter-VPC traffic out through NAT gateways and internet gateways sends traffic over the public internet, which is both insecure and not an efficient or intended way to interconnect VPCs that belong to the same organization.

o.t: Deploy VPN gateways in each VPC. Create a transit VPC in the networking team’s AWS account to connect to each VPC.
o.w: The legacy 'transit VPC' approach using self-managed VPN gateways and EC2-based routing software requires manually managing and scaling VPN tunnels and routing appliances, which is significantly more operational overhead than the fully managed AWS Transit Gateway.

explain: AWS Transit Gateway: It is designed to simplify the connectivity between multiple VPCs. It acts as a central hub that allows you to connect multiple VPCs and on-premises networks. This approach reduces the complexity of managing peering connections individually.

q: An IAM user made several configuration changes to AWS resources in their company's account during a production deployment last week. A solutions architect learned that a couple of security group rules are not configured as desired. The solutions architect wants to confirm which IAM user was responsible for making changes. Which service should the solutions architect use to find the desired information?

o.t: Amazon Inspector
o.w: Amazon Inspector assesses workloads for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure; it does not log who made configuration changes to AWS resources.

o.t: AWS Config
o.w: AWS Config tracks and shows the history of a resource's configuration changes over time, but it does not record which specific IAM identity made each underlying API call the way CloudTrail does.

o.t: AWS CloudTrail
o.w: AWS CloudTrail records every API call made in the account, including the identity of the caller, making it the definitive service for determining exactly which IAM user made the security group configuration changes.

o.t: Amazon GuardDuty
o.w: Amazon GuardDuty is a threat-detection service that analyzes logs for malicious or anomalous activity; it is not designed to answer straightforward 'who changed this configuration' questions.

explain: AWS CloudTrail is a service provided by Amazon Web Services (AWS) that allows you to monitor and log AWS account activity. It records API calls made on your AWS account, capturing information such as the identity of the caller, the time of the API call, the source IP address, the request parameters, and the response elements returned by the AWS service.

q: A company has 5 PB of archived data on physical tapes. The company needs to preserve the data on the tapes for another 10 years for compliance purposes. The company wants to migrate to AWS in the next 6 months. The data center that stores the tapes has a 1 Gbps uplink internet connectivity. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

o.t: Configure an on-premises Tape Gateway. Create virtual tapes in the AWS Cloud. Use backup software to copy the physical tape to the virtual tape.
o.w: Copying 5 PB of tape data to a virtual Tape Gateway still requires transferring it over the existing 1 Gbps internet uplink, which at that bandwidth would take far too long to complete within the 6-month window.

o.t: Order multiple AWS Snowball devices that have Tape Gateway. Copy the physical tapes to virtual tapes in Snowball. Ship the Snowball devices to AWS. Create a lifecycle policy to move the tapes to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
